title: Insurance Claims Are AI's Messiest Data Problem — Denys Linkov, Wisedocs
talk_summary: A Wisedocs AI lead describes how messy, heterogeneous insurance claim documents (PDFs, faxes, 8GB files, duplicates, conflicting diagnoses) are handled with a layered pipeline: OCR/preprocessing, extraction models, classifiers, a summary layer, human verification, then higher-level analysis. He emphasizes calibrated evals (MLCR benchmark with conciseness/accuracy/completeness axes, triple-judge verification), human-in-the-loop, and using cheap specialized models rather than LLMs for everything.

takeaways.technique: Multi-axis calibrated eval with judge verification
takeaways.what_they_do: They score model outputs on three separate axes (conciseness, accuracy, completeness) against human-expert-validated answers, using a calibrated set of judges with triple-judge verification, and keep a private held-out set to prevent benchmark overfitting.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we do the triple judge uh verification ... this is based on a human verified answer and on a calibrated set of judges
takeaways.numbers: Highest accuracy on hard reasoning tiers went from 20% to 75% within a few months as models improved

takeaways.technique: Specialized small models over LLMs for extraction/classification
takeaways.what_they_do: They split the AI work into classification/extraction (trained own models, cheaper, lower hallucination) versus complex decision tasks, reserving LLMs for the high-value top of the pipeline.
takeaways.evidence_quote: LLMs are not the right solution for everything ... for us cost is really important. So, that's why we trained our own models

takeaways.technique: Abstraction/summary layer that concentrates information density
takeaways.what_they_do: They build a layered pipeline where each stage (OCR -> extraction -> classifiers -> summary) compresses and concentrates information, verified at each step, so the top-level model only sees dense, verified context rather than raw huge documents.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we have this abstraction pattern that sort of concentrates the the density of information as you go up, um but it's verified at various points
takeaways.numbers: Cited 8GB PDFs that blow past any context window

takeaways.what_they_do: The system surfaces specific discrepancies (e.g., conflicting diagnosis with page references) for a human to adjudicate rather than making the final call, which they say removes most regulatory/quality risk.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we surface these insights ... on page two on page 20, there there's a difference of diagnosis ... you should take a look
takeaways.numbers: Claims human-in-the-loop removes ~70% of regulatory concerns

takeaways.technique: Deduplicate and detect repeated/commingled inputs before processing
takeaways.what_they_do: They invest in detection systems for duplicate records (up to 50% in some jurisdictions) and commingled/mismatched records before downstream processing, because bad upstream data poisons everything.
takeaways.evidence_quote: unless you have good systems to detect this, you got you just keep getting the same bad quality data
takeaways.numbers: Duplicates can be as much as 50% or higher in some jurisdictions

takeaways.technique: Cost-aware Pareto routing with published cost curves
takeaways.what_they_do: They track cost-per-question against quality on Pareto frontiers and explicitly weigh cost vs accuracy vs completeness per model family (e.g., GPT accurate but incomplete, Anthropic complete but slightly less accurate).
